Fliers, ancient and modern, by weight.Mosquito: Only female mosquitoes bite, because they need blood protein to make eggs; the males feed on nectar.
Fliers, ancient and modern, by weight.Honeybee: A worker bee beats her wings about 230 times a second, and that rapid buzz is the sound of a flying bee.
Fliers, ancient and modern, by weight.Ruby-throated hummingbird: Weighing little more than a penny, it migrates nonstop across the Gulf of Mexico, a flight of roughly 800 km.
Fliers, ancient and modern, by weight.Little brown bat: Hunting with echolocation, one of these bats can catch hundreds of tiny insects in an hour, but white-nose syndrome has devastated the species.
Fliers, ancient and modern, by weight.Barn owl: Its heart-shaped face funnels sound to slightly uneven ears, letting it pinpoint prey in total darkness by hearing alone.
Fliers, ancient and modern, by weight.Golden-crowned flying fox: One of the largest bats in the world, with a wingspan of up to about 1.5 m, it lives in Philippine forests and eats fruit.
Fliers, ancient and modern, by weight.Canada goose: Flocks fly in a V because each bird gets lift from the swirling air off the wingtips of the one ahead, saving energy on long migrations.
Fliers, ancient and modern, by weight.Andean condor: With a wingspan of around 3 m it soars for hours on warm air without flapping, and it can live over 70 years in captivity.
Fliers, ancient and modern, by weight.Argentavis: This extinct giant from Argentina, a relative of vultures, had a wingspan of about 6 to 7 m and lived roughly six million years ago.
Fliers, ancient and modern, by weight.Quetzalcoatlus: Named for the feathered serpent god Quetzalcoatl, this Cretaceous pterosaur stood as tall as a giraffe, with a wingspan of around 10 m.

How tall these towers are.Leaning Tower of Pisa: Construction began in 1173 and the soft soil began tilting it within years; a 1990s-2001 engineering fix reduced the lean without straightening it.
How tall these towers are.Blackpool Tower: Opened in 1894 and modelled on the Eiffel Tower, it has a ballroom at its base that is still in use.
How tall these towers are.Space Needle, Seattle: Built for the 1962 World's Fair in under a year, its revolving restaurant turns a full circle in about 47 minutes.
How tall these towers are.Eiffel Tower: Gustave Eiffel's tower was meant to stand for only 20 years after the 1889 World's Fair, but its use as a radio mast saved it.
How tall these towers are.Berlin TV Tower: Opened in 1969 in East Berlin, sunlight on its steel sphere makes a cross-shaped glint, nicknamed the Pope's Revenge by locals.
How tall these towers are.Oriental Pearl, Shanghai: Its pink spheres were a symbol of 1990s Shanghai, and its design is said to echo pearls falling on a jade plate in a Chinese poem.
How tall these towers are.Ostankino Tower, Moscow: Completed in 1967, it was the tallest freestanding structure in the world until the CN Tower took the record.
How tall these towers are.CN Tower, Toronto: It held the record as the world's tallest freestanding structure from 1976 until 2007, and lightning strikes it dozens of times a year.
How tall these towers are.Canton Tower: Its twisting lattice shape earned it the nickname Slim Waist, and it was among the tallest TV towers when completed in 2009.
How tall these towers are.Tokyo Skytree: Opened in 2012, it is a broadcasting tower and the tallest tower in the world; its design blends steel with traditional Japanese curves.

Radioactive isotopes by half-life.Polonium-214: It is part of the uranium-238 decay chain and lasts less than a millisecond.
Radioactive isotopes by half-life.Radon-222: The radioactive gas seeps up from soil into basements, and is a leading cause of lung cancer.
Radioactive isotopes by half-life.Iodine-131: Used to treat thyroid disorders; after nuclear accidents it is taken up by the thyroid, which is why iodine tablets are handed out.
Radioactive isotopes by half-life.Cobalt-60: It is used in radiotherapy and for sterilizing medical equipment and food.
Radioactive isotopes by half-life.Tritium (hydrogen-3): It is the glow in some watch dials and exit signs, and is also studied as a fusion fuel.
Radioactive isotopes by half-life.Strontium-90: Chemically it mimics calcium, so the body deposits it in bones, which makes it a dangerous fallout product.
Radioactive isotopes by half-life.Carbon-14: Radiocarbon dating can date organic remains up to around 50,000 years, earning Willard Libby a Nobel Prize in 1960.
Radioactive isotopes by half-life.Plutonium-239: It fueled the Nagasaki bomb, and is produced in nuclear reactors.
Radioactive isotopes by half-life.Uranium-235: It is the only naturally occurring fissile isotope, making up only about 0.7 percent of natural uranium.
Radioactive isotopes by half-life.Uranium-238: Its half-life is about as long as Earth's age, and depleted uranium is mostly this isotope.

How loud is it? Sounds by decibels.Normal breathing: Each 10 dB step feels about twice as loud, and quiet breathing is near the edge of hearing.
How loud is it? Sounds by decibels.Whisper: Libraries keep quiet at about 30 to 40 dB, around the level of a whisper.
How loud is it? Sounds by decibels.Normal conversation: Normal talk is well within safe hearing, and because the scale is logarithmic, 70 dB carries ten times the energy.
How loud is it? Sounds by decibels.Vacuum cleaner: Not harmful alone, but sound above 85 dB for hours can damage hearing.
How loud is it? Sounds by decibels.Gas lawn mower: Hearing can be damaged after a few hours at this level, so mowing calls for ear protection.
How loud is it? Sounds by decibels.Rock concert: Hearing damage can occur within minutes at this level, so earplugs are a good idea at gigs.
How loud is it? Sounds by decibels.Nearby thunderclap: Lightning heats the air to about 30,000 degrees, and that explosive expansion produces the thunder.
How loud is it? Sounds by decibels.Threshold of pain: Around this level sound becomes painful, and near 140 dB can cause instant damage.
How loud is it? Sounds by decibels.Jet takeoff up close: Ground crews wear double hearing protection near jets, as a takeoff up close is around 140 to 150 dB.
How loud is it? Sounds by decibels.Rocket launch: Launch pads flood water to dampen the roar, because the sound could damage the rocket itself.

How these missions ended.Skylab falls to Earth: America's first space station fell in July 1979, scattering debris across the Indian Ocean and western Australia, where a town fined NASA for littering.
How these missions ended.Magellan dives into Venus: Magellan mapped about 98 percent of Venus with radar through the clouds, then was deliberately sent into the atmosphere to test how it behaved in the thick air.
How these missions ended.Mir is deorbited: The Russian station Mir stayed up for 15 years, far beyond its planned lifespan, and was guided into the South Pacific's spacecraft graveyard.
How these missions ended.Galileo plunges into Jupiter: Galileo was steered into Jupiter to avoid ever contaminating Europa, a moon that may hide a subsurface ocean suitable for life.
How these missions ended.MESSENGER hits Mercury: MESSENGER became the first spacecraft to orbit Mercury and, out of fuel after four years, crashed onto the surface, leaving a new crater about 16 meters wide.
How these missions ended.Rosetta lands on its comet: Rosetta's lander Philae bounced and landed in shadow on comet 67P, and a year later Rosetta itself touched down there to end the mission.
How these missions ended.Cassini dives into Saturn: Cassini spent 13 years at Saturn and was sent into its atmosphere to protect moons like Enceladus, whose hidden ocean it had helped reveal.
How these missions ended.Dawn falls silent: Dawn is the only spacecraft to orbit two bodies in the asteroid belt, Vesta and Ceres, and it stopped when it ran out of the hydrazine fuel for steering.
How these missions ended.Spitzer switched off: Spitzer was an infrared telescope that found seven Earth-size planets around the star TRAPPIST-1, and it trailed Earth in orbit rather than circling it.
How these missions ended.Ingenuity's last flight: This small helicopter was meant to fly five times on Mars but managed 72 flights, proving that powered flight is possible in the thin Martian air.

Big ideas in Earth science, in order.Hutton's Theory of the Earth: James Hutton argued that Earth is immensely old, shaped by slow processes, and saw 'no vestige of a beginning, no prospect of an end'.
Big ideas in Earth science, in order.Beaufort wind scale: Admiral Francis Beaufort created his scale of wind force, from 0 for calm to 12 for hurricane, based on observing sailing ships' sails.
Big ideas in Earth science, in order.Mohs hardness scale: Friedrich Mohs ranked minerals from talc at 1 to diamond at 10, simply by which can scratch which, and it remains a field tool.
Big ideas in Earth science, in order.Lyell's Principles of Geology: Charles Lyell's book argued that the same slow processes we see today shaped the Earth, and it deeply influenced Charles Darwin.
Big ideas in Earth science, in order.Agassiz's Ice Age theory: Louis Agassiz proposed that huge ice sheets once covered much of Europe, which at first seemed to many scientists absurd.
Big ideas in Earth science, in order.Wegener's continental drift: Alfred Wegener proposed that continents move, but he could not explain how, and his idea was ridiculed until the 1960s.
Big ideas in Earth science, in order.Richter magnitude scale: Charles Richter's scale measured earthquake size using a seismograph, and was developed with Beno Gutenberg for California quakes.
Big ideas in Earth science, in order.Seafloor magnetic stripes: Stripes of alternating magnetic direction in the seafloor, found in 1963 by Vine and Matthews, provided key evidence for seafloor spreading.
Big ideas in Earth science, in order.Saffir–Simpson scale: The Saffir-Simpson scale, devised by an engineer and a meteorologist, ranks hurricanes in five categories by wind speed.
Big ideas in Earth science, in order.Alvarez asteroid hypothesis: Luis and Walter Alvarez pointed to a layer of iridium in rock as evidence that an asteroid caused the dinosaurs' extinction.

Minimum legal aging for these drinks.Blanco tequila: The agave spirit is bottled fresh or rested under two months; it tastes closest to the raw blue Weber agave it is distilled from.
Minimum legal aging for these drinks.Reposado tequila: The Spanish word means 'rested': this tequila sits in oak for between two months and a year, mellowing and picking up a pale gold colour.
Minimum legal aging for these drinks.Añejo tequila: The name means 'aged' in Spanish; it spends one to three years in small oak barrels, which turns it amber and smooth.
Minimum legal aging for these drinks.Non-vintage Champagne: The rule includes 12 months on the lees, the yeast sediment, which gives Champagne its bready aroma; vintage bottles must wait three years.
Minimum legal aging for these drinks.Straight bourbon: US law demands the whisky be aged in new charred oak, and 'straight' is the label for two years or more with no added colouring.
Minimum legal aging for these drinks.Scotch whisky: By law it must mature at least three years in oak casks in Scotland, otherwise it cannot be called Scotch.
Minimum legal aging for these drinks.Cognac VSOP: The letters stand for 'Very Superior Old Pale', and the youngest brandy in the blend must be at least four years old.
Minimum legal aging for these drinks.Rioja Gran Reserva (red): A red marked this way must age at least five years in total, including at least two years in oak, before release.
Minimum legal aging for these drinks.Cognac XO: Short for 'Extra Old', and since 2018 the youngest eau-de-vie in an XO must be at least ten years old, not six.
Minimum legal aging for these drinks.Balsamico Extravecchio: Traditional balsamic vinegar from Modena is aged in a series of barrels of different woods, and the Extravecchio grade means 25 years or more.

Sinners in Dante's Inferno, from the gat.The fence-sitters: The uncommitted, who never took sides in life, chase a blank banner forever while wasps and hornets sting them.
Sinners in Dante's Inferno, from the gat.Virtuous pagans: Limbo is home to Homer, Socrates and other good people who were never baptised; Dante's guide Virgil lives here too.
Sinners in Dante's Inferno, from the gat.The lustful: They are blown about endlessly by a violent storm, as passion swept them in life, and Francesca da Rimini tells her story here.
Sinners in Dante's Inferno, from the gat.The gluttonous: They lie in a foul, freezing rain and mud while Cerberus, the three-headed hound, claws and tears at them.
Sinners in Dante's Inferno, from the gat.Hoarders and wasters: Two groups push heavy weights against each other in a half circle, shouting 'Why do you hoard?' and 'Why do you waste?'
Sinners in Dante's Inferno, from the gat.The wrathful: Sunk in the muddy river Styx they tear each other to pieces, while the sullen lie beneath the surface, gurgling.
Sinners in Dante's Inferno, from the gat.Heretics: Locked in flaming tombs within the walled city of Dis, they include Epicureans who believed the soul dies with the body.
Sinners in Dante's Inferno, from the gat.The violent: Divided into three rings, for violence against neighbours, oneself and God; the suicides are turned into thorny trees.
Sinners in Dante's Inferno, from the gat.Frauds: Malebolge is a set of ten ditches, home to seducers, flatterers, thieves and corrupt politicians, each with their own tailored torment.
Sinners in Dante's Inferno, from the gat.Traitors: They are frozen in the ice of Cocytus at the centre of Hell, where Satan chews on Judas, Brutus and Cassius.

Famous fictional cats, by first appearan.Puss in Boots: Charles Perrault's 1697 tale has a clever cat who tricks an ogre into turning into a mouse, and then eats him.
Famous fictional cats, by first appearan.The Cheshire Cat: Only its grin remains after it vanishes, and the phrase 'grinning like a Cheshire cat' was already in use before Lewis Carroll.
Famous fictional cats, by first appearan.Tom Kitten: Beatrix Potter's kitten bursts out of his clothes, and they are then picked up by a family of ducks.
Famous fictional cats, by first appearan.Macavity: T. S. Eliot's 'Mystery Cat' from Old Possum's Book of Practical Cats, modelled on a criminal mastermind, then inspired the musical Cats.
Famous fictional cats, by first appearan.The Cat in the Hat: Dr Seuss wrote it using only 236 different words, as a challenge to replace the dull school primers of the day.
Famous fictional cats, by first appearan.Behemoth (Bulgakov): A giant talking black cat in Bulgakov's The Master and Margarita who walks on his hind legs and plays chess.
Famous fictional cats, by first appearan.Mog: Judith Kerr, a refugee from Nazi Germany, created this forgetful family cat, and also wrote The Tiger Who Came to Tea.
Famous fictional cats, by first appearan.Garfield: Jim Davis named him after his own grandfather, James Garfield Davis, and the cat's lasagna obsession became famous.
Famous fictional cats, by first appearan.Crookshanks: Hermione's orange half-Kneazle cat in Prisoner of Azkaban, which could tell Scabbers was really Peter Pettigrew.
Famous fictional cats, by first appearan.Pete the Cat: The picture book by Eric Litwin and James Dean shows a blue cat who keeps singing as he steps in strawberries and mud.

Calories per 100 grams.Cucumber: About 95 percent water, it stays near the bottom of any calorie ranking.
Calories per 100 grams.Apple: About 85 percent water, an apple floats because roughly a quarter of its volume is air.
Calories per 100 grams.Banana: Bananas are slightly radioactive from natural potassium-40, which is harmless.
Calories per 100 grams.Cooked white rice: Cooked rice soaks up water, which is why it has about a third of the calories of the same weight of dry rice.
Calories per 100 grams.Cooked chicken breast: Among the leanest meats, cooked chicken breast offers about 31 grams of protein per 100 grams.
Calories per 100 grams.White bread: White bread is about a third water by weight, and its starchy crumb makes it the middling choice here.
Calories per 100 grams.Granulated sugar: Pure carbohydrate has about 4 calories per gram, the same as the carbohydrate in an apple.
Calories per 100 grams.Peanut butter: Peanuts are legumes, not true nuts, and about half of peanut butter's weight is fat.
Calories per 100 grams.Butter: Butter is roughly 80 percent fat, which explains why it is so dense in calories.
Calories per 100 grams.Olive oil: As pure fat, it provides about 9 calories per gram, more than double protein or carbohydrate.

Comets by orbital period.Comet Encke: Pierre Méchain first saw it in 1786, and Johann Encke worked out its orbit; it has one of the shortest periods of any known comet.
Comets by orbital period.Tempel 1: NASA's Deep Impact fired a copper probe into it in 2005 to look inside the comet.
Comets by orbital period.Tempel-Tuttle: It is the parent of the Leonid meteor shower, which produced spectacular meteor storms in 1833 and 1966.
Comets by orbital period.Pons-Brooks: Nicknamed the Devil Comet for horn-like outbursts of gas, it was visible in 2024.
Comets by orbital period.Halley's Comet: Edmond Halley predicted its return, which happened in 1758 after his death; the last visit was 1986, the next due in 2061.
Comets by orbital period.Swift-Tuttle: The parent of the August Perseid meteor shower, its nucleus is about 26 km wide, bigger than the asteroid that ended the dinosaurs.
Comets by orbital period.Ikeya-Zhang: Amateurs Kaoru Ikeya and Zhang Daqing found it in 2002, and it was later linked to a comet seen in 1661.
Comets by orbital period.Hale-Bopp: Two amateurs found it independently in 1995, and it was visible to the naked eye for about 18 months.
Comets by orbital period.Comet NEOWISE: It was found by NASA's NEOWISE space telescope in March 2020 and became the brightest comet in northern skies in decades.
Comets by orbital period.Hyakutake: Japanese amateur Yuji Hyakutake found it in 1996, when it passed close to Earth and its tail stretched across much of the sky.

Pieces in the game box.Yahtzee dice: A Yahtzee, five of a kind in a single roll, comes up about once in 1,296 tries.
Pieces in the game box.Checkers pieces: Each side has 12; computers 'solved' the game as a draw in 2007.
Pieces in the game box.Double-six dominoes: Each of the 28 tiles is a unique pair of numbers from 0 to 6.
Pieces in the game box.Backgammon checkers: One of the oldest board games still played, with ancestors dating back about 5,000 years.
Pieces in the game box.Chess pieces: The number of possible chess games exceeds the number of atoms in the observable universe.
Pieces in the game box.Connect Four discs: The 7 by 6 grid was solved in 1988: the first player can always force a win.
Pieces in the game box.Jenga blocks: Created by Leslie Scott, its name is Swahili for 'build'.
Pieces in the game box.Scrabble tiles: Alfred Butts devised the letter counts by analyzing the frequency of letters in newspapers like the New York Times.
Pieces in the game box.Classic Uno cards: It was created in 1971 by an Ohio barber named Merle Robbins.
Pieces in the game box.Mahjong tiles: The Chinese name, mahjong, means 'sparrow', and shuffling is said to sound like chirping birds.

Top speeds, from crawl to blur.Garden snail: A garden snail glides on a slime trail at roughly 50 meters per hour. That slime also lets it crawl over razor blades unharmed.
Top speeds, from crawl to blur.Three-toed sloth: Its slow pace saves energy, and algae grow in its fur, tinting it green as camouflage. It climbs down from the trees only about once a week.
Top speeds, from crawl to blur.American cockroach: Cockroaches can briefly run much faster and are known to survive weeks without food. They also can live for a week with their head removed.
Top speeds, from crawl to blur.House mouse: Mice are speedy for their size, and they are good climbers and jumpers, and they can squeeze through gaps about the width of a pencil.
Top speeds, from crawl to blur.African elephant: The largest living land animal usually walks, but can reach about 25 km/h in a fast trot. It can't jump, however.
Top speeds, from crawl to blur.Usain Bolt: His 2009 world record 100 meters in 9.58 seconds averaged about 37 km/h, and his top burst reached around 44 km/h.
Top speeds, from crawl to blur.Grizzly bear: Surprisingly quick for a heavy animal, it can charge at this speed, though only for short distances. Its claws can be as long as a human finger.
Top speeds, from crawl to blur.Racehorse: Every modern Thoroughbred traces back to three Arabian stallions imported to England around the 1700s, bred for sprint speed ever since.
Top speeds, from crawl to blur.Pronghorn: The fastest land animal in North America can sustain high speeds over many kilometers, far longer than a cheetah, to outrun ancient predators.
Top speeds, from crawl to blur.Cheetah: The fastest land animal on Earth can accelerate from 0 to 100 km/h in about three seconds, but it can sustain the sprint for only a few hundred meters.

When these oddball snacks were born.Jell-O: Its inventor reportedly sold the rights to this gelatin dessert for just $450, and it later became a household name.
When these oddball snacks were born.Marshmallow Fluff: This marshmallow spread comes from Massachusetts, where a yearly festival celebrates the Fluffernutter sandwich.
When these oddball snacks were born.Pez: The name of this Austrian-born candy comes from Pfefferminz, German for peppermint, and the first ones were marketed as an alternative to smoking.
When these oddball snacks were born.Twinkie: The cream-filled sponge cake reportedly got its name from a St. Louis billboard for Twinkle Toes shoes.
When these oddball snacks were born.Spam: Hormel's canned meat is hugely popular in Hawaii, Korea and the Philippines, and it was supplied to troops in World War II.
When these oddball snacks were born.Cheetos: Charles Elmer Doolin of the Frito company launched this puffed corn snack, and its orange dust inspired mascot Chester Cheetah.
When these oddball snacks were born.Cheez Whiz: Kraft's spreadable cheese came out in 1952, and it was developed by a food scientist, not a cheesemaker.
When these oddball snacks were born.Pop-Tarts: Kellogg's rushed these toaster pastries out to compete with a rival product from Post, and the name nods to pop art.
When these oddball snacks were born.Pringles: Fredric Baur designed the stackable can, and he requested that part of his ashes be buried in one after he died in 2008.
When these oddball snacks were born.Lunchables: Oscar Mayer launched these boxed lunch kits in 1988, pitching them as an easy way to put together a meal.

Odysseus's adventures on the way home.Lotus-Eaters: Eating the lotus made men forget about going home; Odysseus had to drag his crew back to the ships.
Odysseus's adventures on the way home.Polyphemus the Cyclops: He told the giant his name was 'Nobody', so when he was blinded, his neighbours said no one was hurting him.
Odysseus's adventures on the way home.Aeolus and his bag of winds: The wind-keeper gave him a bag of winds, but his crew opened it near Ithaca, thinking it held treasure, and blew them off course.
Odysseus's adventures on the way home.Laestrygonian giants: These cannibal giants sank all of his ships except Odysseus's own.
Odysseus's adventures on the way home.Circe: The sorceress turned his men into pigs; Hermes gave Odysseus the herb moly so he could resist her magic.
Odysseus's adventures on the way home.Visit to the Underworld: He visited the dead to consult the prophet Tiresias and met his mother and Achilles.
Odysseus's adventures on the way home.Sirens: Odysseus had his crew plug their ears with beeswax and tied himself to the mast so he could hear the song.
Odysseus's adventures on the way home.Scylla and Charybdis: A six-headed monster and a whirlpool guarded opposite sides of the strait; 'between Scylla and Charybdis' became an idiom.
Odysseus's adventures on the way home.Cattle of the Sun: His hungry crew ate the sun god's sacred cattle, and Zeus destroyed their ship; only Odysseus survived.
Odysseus's adventures on the way home.Calypso's island: The nymph kept him on her island for seven years and offered immortality, but he longed for home.

When these animation studios were founde.Walt Disney Studio: It started as a small cartoon studio, and its breakthrough was Mickey Mouse, who first appeared in 1928.
When these animation studios were founde.Hanna-Barbera: Two creators of Tom and Jerry founded it, and its The Flintstones became the first prime-time animated sitcom.
When these animation studios were founde.Aardman: The Bristol studio behind Wallace and Gromit works in plasticine, and animators shoot a few seconds of film in a day.
When these animation studios were founde.Studio Ghibli: Its name comes from an Italian word for a hot Saharan wind, and Spirited Away won it an Oscar.
When these animation studios were founde.Pixar: Steve Jobs bought it from Lucasfilm for 5 million dollars, and in 1995 it released Toy Story, the first fully computer-animated feature.
When these animation studios were founde.Blue Sky Studios: It made the Ice Age films, and was shut down by Disney in 2021 after buying its parent studio.
When these animation studios were founde.DreamWorks: Steven Spielberg, Jeffrey Katzenberg and David Geffen founded it, and its big breakthrough in animation was Shrek.
When these animation studios were founde.Cartoon Saloon: This Irish studio in Kilkenny makes hand-drawn films, such as The Secret of Kells, and has several Oscar nominations.
When these animation studios were founde.Laika: The Oregon studio behind Coraline pioneered 3D-printed faces for its stop-motion puppets.
When these animation studios were founde.Illumination: Founded by Chris Meledandri, it made Despicable Me, whose Minions became a hit, and The Super Mario Bros. Movie.

Size of the playing area.Table tennis table: It began as a Victorian after-dinner parlor game, played with books as a net.
Size of the playing area.Sumo ring: The dohyo is a raised clay ring about 4.5 m across, purified with salt before bouts.
Size of the playing area.Boxing ring: It is square despite the name, which comes from crowds forming a ring around old bare-knuckle fights.
Size of the playing area.Badminton court: Its shuttlecocks fly over 400 km/h in the fastest smashes.
Size of the playing area.Volleyball court: William Morgan invented it in 1895 as a gentler alternative to basketball.
Size of the playing area.Tennis court (doubles): Its extra 'tramlines' on each side only count in doubles play.
Size of the playing area.Basketball court (FIBA): James Naismith invented the game in 1891 using peach baskets.
Size of the playing area.NHL ice rink: The rink is 200 ft by 85 ft with rounded corners, narrower than an Olympic rink.
Size of the playing area.Soccer pitch: The rules give a range of sizes rather than a fixed one, so no two pitches need be identical.
Size of the playing area.Polo field: The largest field in any ball sport, and players change ponies between periods.

How long these take.Microwave popcorn: The water in each kernel turns to steam and bursts the hull at about 180 °C, which is what makes the pop.
How long these take.Soft-boiled egg: Egg proteins set at different temperatures, so the white firms up before the yolk does, giving the runny center.
How long these take.A Pomodoro work session: The name is Italian for tomato, after the tomato-shaped kitchen timer that Francesco Cirillo used as a student.
How long these take.A soccer match: Though the game lasts 90 minutes plus stoppages, the ball is typically in play for only around an hour.
How long these take.Elite men's marathon: Kelvin Kiptum's record is just over two hours, a pace of around 21 km/h sustained for the whole 42 kilometers.
How long these take.Flight, London to New York: Jet stream tailwinds make the flight west to east about an hour or so shorter than the return trip.
How long these take.Le Mans endurance race: Drivers share each car in shifts over a full day and night on a track in France, and the winner is whoever covers the most laps.
How long these take.Moon's orbit around Earth: The Moon takes 27.3 days to orbit, but the cycle of phases takes 29.5 since Earth also moves around the Sun.
How long these take.Human pregnancy: Human pregnancy lasts about 40 weeks, but elephants take about 22 months, the longest of any land mammal.
How long these take.A year on Mars: It takes 687 Earth days, roughly 1.9 Earth years, because Mars is farther from the Sun and moves more slowly.

How old are these games and toys?.Senet: Senet is an Egyptian board game, found in Tutankhamun's tomb and played for thousands of years, though its exact rules are lost.
How old are these games and toys?.Royal Game of Ur: A Babylonian clay tablet preserves its rules, deciphered by Irving Finkel, and boards were found in royal tombs at Ur by Leonard Woolley.
How old are these games and toys?.Yo-yo: Greek vases show it, and in the Philippines it became a hunting weapon; the word yo-yo is probably Filipino.
How old are these games and toys?.Chaturanga (early chess): This Indian war game, named for the four divisions of the army, infantry, cavalry, elephants and chariots, was the ancestor of chess.
How old are these games and toys?.Playing cards: Cards appeared in China around this time and spread west through Egypt, where the suits included cups and coins.
How old are these games and toys?.Jigsaw puzzle: London mapmaker John Spilsbury made the first one, gluing a map to wood and cutting out countries to teach geography.
How old are these games and toys?.Teddy bear: It's named for President Theodore Roosevelt, who refused to shoot a tied-up bear on a 1902 hunting trip.
How old are these games and toys?.Crossword puzzle: The first appeared in the New York World, on December 21, 1913, diamond-shaped, and was called a word-cross.
How old are these games and toys?.Frisbee: It grew from pie tins from the Frisbie Baking Company that students tossed around; Wham-O launched the plastic disc in 1957.
How old are these games and toys?.Rubik's Cube: Hungarian Ernő Rubik invented it as a teaching tool for 3D geometry, and it has about 43 quintillion possible positions.

When these quirky celebrations began.El Colacho (baby jumping): Men dressed as devils leap over babies lying on mattresses in the Spanish village of Castrillo de Murcia, to cleanse them of original sin.
When these quirky celebrations began.Night of the Radishes: In Oaxaca, Mexico, every December 23, carvers turn giant radishes into sculptures of nativity scenes and other scenes.
When these quirky celebrations began.La Tomatina: Thousands of people throw about a hundred tonnes of tomatoes at one another in Buñol, Spain, each last Wednesday of August.
When these quirky celebrations began.Burning Man: It began as a bonfire at San Francisco's Baker Beach, burning a wooden figure; it later moved to Nevada's Black Rock Desert.
When these quirky celebrations began.Pi Day: Larry Shaw started it at San Francisco's Exploratorium; March 14 is 3/14, and it falls on Einstein's birthday.
When these quirky celebrations began.Monkey Buffet Festival: Lopburi, Thailand, lays out tonnes of fruit and sweets for the macaques living around its old temples.
When these quirky celebrations began.Talk Like a Pirate Day: Two Americans, John Baur and Mark Summers, invented it; humorist Dave Barry's column spread it worldwide, and it's observed on September 19.
When these quirky celebrations began.Boryeong Mud Festival: South Korea's festival promotes cosmetics made with local mud, and draws crowds in the hundreds of thousands to wrestle and slide in it.
When these quirky celebrations began.Mike the Headless Chicken Fest: The Fruita, Colorado, event honors a chicken that lived about 18 months after beheading in 1945, fed with an eyedropper.
When these quirky celebrations began.Frozen Dead Guy Days: Nederland, Colorado, celebrates a man kept frozen in dry ice in a shed, with coffin races and frozen salmon tosses.

When these countries abolished the death.Venezuela: Venezuela abolished capital punishment for all crimes in 1863, one of the first countries in the world to do so.
When these countries abolished the death.Portugal: Portugal ended the death penalty for civilian crimes in 1867, one of the first European countries to do so.
When these countries abolished the death.Netherlands: The Dutch abolished it for ordinary crimes in 1870, and the last civilian execution had been in 1860.
When these countries abolished the death.Italy: Italy's 1948 constitution ended it for ordinary crimes, and it was fully abolished in 1994.
When these countries abolished the death.West Germany: West Germany's 1949 Basic Law abolished the death penalty, as a direct reaction to the horrors of the Nazi era.
When these countries abolished the death.Canada: Canada's last executions were in 1962, and a narrow free vote in Parliament abolished it in 1976.
When these countries abolished the death.France: President Mitterrand and Justice Minister Robert Badinter abolished it in 1981; the last guillotine execution was in 1977.
When these countries abolished the death.South Africa: South Africa's Constitutional Court ruled in 1995 that capital punishment violated the new constitution.
When these countries abolished the death.Turkey: Turkey abolished the death penalty in 2004, as part of its long bid to join the European Union.
When these countries abolished the death.Mexico: Mexico abolished the death penalty for all crimes in 2005; its last execution was carried out in 1957.

How old is it? Rocks and landscapes.Jack Hills zircons: Tiny crystals from Western Australia are the oldest known pieces of Earth's own material, hinting that crust and water existed very early.
How old is it? Rocks and landscapes.Acasta Gneiss: Found in northwestern Canada, it is among the oldest known intact rock on Earth.
How old is it? Rocks and landscapes.Uluru's sandstone: Most of the great rock lies underground, with sandstone layers tilted almost vertical.
How old is it? Rocks and landscapes.Appalachians start rising: These mountains were once as tall as the Himalayas. Hundreds of millions of years of erosion have worn them down.
How old is it? Rocks and landscapes.Rocky Mountains rise: Raised in a mountain-building event called the Laramide orogeny, which happened late in the age of dinosaurs.
How old is it? Rocks and landscapes.Himalayas start rising: Still growing by a few millimetres a year as the Indian plate pushes into Asia.
How old is it? Rocks and landscapes.Grand Canyon carved: The Colorado River carved the canyon, and the rocks exposed at its bottom are about 1.8 billion years old.
How old is it? Rocks and landscapes.Great Lakes take shape: Shaped as ice-age glaciers retreated. Together the lakes hold about a fifth of the world's surface fresh water.
How old is it? Rocks and landscapes.Paricutín volcano born: A farmer named Dionisio Pulido watched it appear in his Mexican cornfield in 1943. It grew 336 metres in its first year.
How old is it? Rocks and landscapes.Newest land on Hawaii: The 2018 Kilauea eruption poured lava into the ocean, adding fresh land to the Big Island's coast.

Maximum takeoff weights of aircraft.Wright Flyer: The first flight lasted only 12 seconds and covered 37 meters, a distance shorter than a modern jumbo jet's wingspan.
Maximum takeoff weights of aircraft.Cessna 172: The most-produced aircraft ever, this small trainer is a flight-school favorite, with over 44,000 built since the 1950s.
Maximum takeoff weights of aircraft.Boeing 737-800: The 737 family is the best-selling jet airliner in history, and the 800 version is among its most common models.
Maximum takeoff weights of aircraft.Boeing 707-320B: Boeing's first big commercial jet helped launch the jet age and made transatlantic flights routine for ordinary passengers.
Maximum takeoff weights of aircraft.Concorde: The supersonic airliner flew at twice the speed of sound and crossed the Atlantic in about three and a half hours.
Maximum takeoff weights of aircraft.Boeing 787-9: Built largely from carbon-fiber composites instead of aluminum, the Dreamliner has big windows that dim at the touch of a button.
Maximum takeoff weights of aircraft.Boeing 777-300ER: A long-range twin-jet with the largest jet engines ever fitted to an aircraft, each wide enough to swallow a 737's body.
Maximum takeoff weights of aircraft.Boeing 747-8: The 'Queen of the Skies' has a distinctive upper-deck hump, and this latest version is the longest passenger airliner ever.
Maximum takeoff weights of aircraft.Airbus A380: The double-decker superjumbo can carry about 850 passengers in an all-economy layout, though typical airlines seat around 500.
Maximum takeoff weights of aircraft.Antonov An-225: The huge Ukrainian cargo plane was the heaviest aircraft ever built, with six engines, and it was destroyed in 2022.

Baseball's famous moments.Babe Ruth's called shot: In the 1932 World Series, Ruth supposedly pointed toward center field before homering, though whether he did is still debated.
Baseball's famous moments.Gehrig's farewell speech: Dying of ALS, he called himself 'the luckiest man on the face of the earth'.
Baseball's famous moments.Shot Heard 'Round the World: Bobby Thomson's home run won the National League pennant for the Giants over the Dodgers.
Baseball's famous moments.Larsen's World Series perfecto: He remains the only pitcher to throw a perfect game in the World Series.
Baseball's famous moments.Mazeroski's walk-off: It remains the only walk-off home run to end a Game 7 of the World Series.
Baseball's famous moments.Buckner's error: A ground ball slipped through Bill Buckner's legs in Game 6 as the Red Sox neared a title, and the Mets won.
Baseball's famous moments.Kirk Gibson's limping homer: Hobbled by injuries, he pinch-hit a homer to win Game 1 for the Dodgers, who went on to win the Series.
Baseball's famous moments.Joe Carter's walk-off: It ended the World Series for Toronto, only the second series ending in a walk-off after Mazeroski's.
Baseball's famous moments.Red Sox break the curse: After 86 years, Boston won, coming back from 0 to 3 down against the Yankees in the ALCS.
Baseball's famous moments.Cubs end their drought: The Cubs won their first title since 1908, a 108-year drought, in a ten-inning Game 7 after a rain delay.

US and UK liquid measures.Tablespoon: Australia's tablespoon is bigger than the US one, at 20 ml, so a recipe written there needs conversion.
US and UK liquid measures.Jigger: The standard bar jigger holds 1.5 US fluid ounces, and cocktail recipes are often built on this single measure.
US and UK liquid measures.UK gill: A gill is a quarter of an imperial pint, and the word is pronounced with a soft g, like Jill.
US and UK liquid measures.US cup: In the US, a cup is 8 fluid ounces, but Australia's metric cup is 250 ml, so bakers can get slightly different results.
US and UK liquid measures.US pint: The US pint is only 16 fluid ounces, which is why an American pint of beer is noticeably smaller than a British one.
US and UK liquid measures.UK pint: The legal measure for draught beer in British pubs, it holds 20 imperial fluid ounces, four more than the US pint.
US and UK liquid measures.US quart: The name comes from being a quarter of a gallon, and it holds two US pints.
US and UK liquid measures.UK quart: It equals two imperial pints, and the imperial system it comes from was defined in Britain in 1824.
US and UK liquid measures.US gallon: It descends from the old English wine gallon of 231 cubic inches, which the US kept after Britain changed its measure.
US and UK liquid measures.UK gallon: Defined in 1824 as the volume of ten pounds of water, it is about a fifth bigger than its American cousin.

Storage media by capacity.5.25-inch floppy (DD): Floppy disks were floppy inside: a flexible magnetic sheet was in a case, and 360 KB holds a few text documents.
Storage media by capacity.5.25-inch floppy (HD): The high-density version doubled the capacity, and drives needed special media to write it.
Storage media by capacity.3.5-inch floppy (HD): This hard-cased disk is the origin of the Save icon, and its 1.44 MB is smaller than a single photo today.
Storage media by capacity.Zip disk: Iomega's cartridge was a hit, though the "click of death" failure ruined many of them.
Storage media by capacity.CD-ROM: A CD was reportedly sized to fit 74 minutes of audio, a length said to fit Beethoven's Ninth Symphony.
Storage media by capacity.DVD: The DVD can hold a movie, and it took its name from digital versatile disc.
Storage media by capacity.Dual-layer DVD: A second data layer on the same side raised DVD capacity to about 8.5 GB.
Storage media by capacity.Blu-ray disc: Its name comes from the blue-violet laser, with a shorter wavelength than red, so it packs data denser.
Storage media by capacity.Dual-layer Blu-ray: Two layers doubled the single-layer capacity of the format to 50 GB.
Storage media by capacity.BDXL triple-layer disc: Three layers made the extended format hold 100 GB, but few drives could read it.

Great libraries, by founding year.Library of Alexandria: Alexandria's library aimed to collect all the world's knowledge, and ships entering the harbor were reportedly searched for books to copy.
Great libraries, by founding year.Vatican Library: The Vatican Library holds over a million printed books and tens of thousands of manuscripts, and it was formally founded by Pope Sixtus IV.
Great libraries, by founding year.Trinity College Library: Trinity's Long Room holds the Book of Kells and a harp said to be Ireland's oldest, and its 65-meter hall is stunning.
Great libraries, by founding year.Bodleian Library (reopened): Thomas Bodley's library at Oxford is a legal deposit library, and readers swear an oath not to set fire to it.
Great libraries, by founding year.Biblioteca Ambrosiana: Milan's Ambrosiana holds Leonardo da Vinci's Codex Atlanticus, a huge collection of his drawings and writings.
Great libraries, by founding year.Library of Congress: The Library of Congress began after a fire in 1814, when Thomas Jefferson sold his personal library to restart it.
Great libraries, by founding year.Boston Public Library: Boston's library was the first large free municipal library in the US, and its Bates Hall has a stunning barrel-vaulted ceiling.
Great libraries, by founding year.New York Public Library: The lions Patience and Fortitude guard the front steps, and the main reading room is among the most famous in the US.
Great libraries, by founding year.The British Library: The British Library moved to its current building in 1998; it holds the Magna Carta and the Gutenberg Bible.
Great libraries, by founding year.Bibliotheca Alexandrina: The new Alexandria library was built as a tribute to the ancient one, and its tilted disk roof is carved with letters from many alphabets.

The missing number in these songs.Mambo No. ___: Pérez Prado wrote the mambo in the 1940s; Lou Bega's 1999 hit went big by naming a roll-call of women: Angela, Pamela, Sandra and others.
The missing number in these songs.___ Nation Army: Jack White has said the title came from how he mispronounced 'Salvation Army' as a child. That famous bassy riff is actually a guitar.
The missing number in these songs.___ Days a Week (Beatles): Ringo Starr reportedly overheard a chauffeur use the phrase and brought it to the band, who turned it into a number one hit.
The missing number in these songs.Love Potion No. ___: The Clovers' 1959 hit was written by Leiber and Stoller, and tells of a fortune-teller's potion that makes everyone fall in love.
The missing number in these songs.When I'm ___ (Beatles): Paul McCartney wrote it as a teenager, long before he and the band recorded it for Sgt. Pepper in 1967.
The missing number in these songs.Summer of '___: Bryan Adams was only nine in 1969. He has hinted that the number is actually a wink at something else, not the year.
The missing number in these songs.___ Problems (Jay-Z): It appeared on The Black Album, built on a Rick Rubin production, and borrows its title line from an earlier Ice-T song.
The missing number in these songs.In the Year ___: The Zager and Evans hit tops a short list of one-hit wonders, holding the US number one spot for six weeks in 1969.
The missing number in these songs.Rent: '___ minutes': The musical Rent counts that figure as the minutes in a non-leap year, and its creator Jonathan Larson died before the show's first public run.
The missing number in these songs.Jenny's number (Tommy Tutone): Tommy Tutone's hit made this phone number famous, and people who really owned it were pestered by callers for years.

Big tech acquisitions.Google buys Android: Google paid about $50 million for the small startup, and Andy Rubin's operating system now runs most of the world's phones.
Big tech acquisitions.Google buys YouTube: Google paid $1.65 billion in stock for the video site, barely a year and a half after it started.
Big tech acquisitions.Microsoft buys Skype: Microsoft paid $8.5 billion, then retired the service in 2025.
Big tech acquisitions.Facebook buys Instagram: Facebook paid about $1 billion for the photo app, which had only 13 employees.
Big tech acquisitions.Facebook buys WhatsApp: Facebook paid about $19 billion for the messaging app, which had around 450 million users.
Big tech acquisitions.Microsoft buys LinkedIn: It cost $26.2 billion, at the time Microsoft's largest acquisition ever.
Big tech acquisitions.Verizon buys Yahoo: Verizon bought the old web giant's core business, and it later became part of a company sold in 2021.
Big tech acquisitions.Microsoft buys GitHub: The $7.5 billion purchase of the code-hosting site worried developers, but it has since grown.
Big tech acquisitions.Musk buys Twitter: The $44 billion deal ended with Musk renaming the platform X in 2023.
Big tech acquisitions.Microsoft buys Activision: At $69 billion, it was the largest gaming deal ever, and regulators took nearly two years to clear it.

Lengths of famous walls.Walls of Dubrovnik: Tall medieval walls up to about 25 m high still ring the old town, which stood in for King's Landing in Game of Thrones.
Lengths of famous walls.Walls of Ávila: Spain's best-preserved medieval walls were built in the 11th and 12th centuries and have 88 towers and nine gates.
Lengths of famous walls.York city walls: England's most complete medieval walls; you can walk much of the top, and the main gates are called bars.
Lengths of famous walls.Theodosian Walls: These shielded Constantinople for nearly a thousand years, until Ottoman cannon finally breached them in 1453.
Lengths of famous walls.Servian Wall, Rome: Tradition credits King Servius Tullius, but they were really built in the 4th century BC after Gauls sacked Rome.
Lengths of famous walls.Aurelian Walls, Rome: Emperor Aurelian ordered them in the 270s as raiders reached Italy; much of the circuit still stands today.
Lengths of famous walls.Antonine Wall: A turf-topped wall across central Scotland built in the AD 140s and abandoned within about 20 years for the line to its south.
Lengths of famous walls.Hadrian's Wall: Begun in AD 122 across northern England, it had a small fort called a milecastle roughly every Roman mile.
Lengths of famous walls.Berlin Wall (full ring): For 28 years from 1961 it encircled West Berlin; the full ring was around 155 km, far longer than the city's famous central section.
Lengths of famous walls.Great Wall of China (all): Not one wall but many, built over two millennia; despite the myth, it can't be seen from the Moon with the naked eye.

Caribbean and Central America, north to.Nassau: Nassau, the capital of the Bahamas, was once a pirate haven. It sits on New Providence Island rather than the larger Grand Bahama.
Caribbean and Central America, north to.Havana: Havana is the largest city in the Caribbean, famous for its vintage American cars that stayed on the road for decades.
Caribbean and Central America, north to.Cancún: Cancún was purpose-built as a resort in the 1970s. Before then, the site was mostly sandbars and a few fishermen's homes.
Caribbean and Central America, north to.Mexico City: Mexico City was built over Lake Texcoco, on the ruins of the Aztec capital Tenochtitlan. It sinks slowly because of the soft ground.
Caribbean and Central America, north to.Santo Domingo: Santo Domingo is the oldest continuously inhabited European settlement in the Americas, founded in 1498 by Columbus's brother.
Caribbean and Central America, north to.Guatemala City: Guatemala City lies in a highland valley ringed by volcanoes. It is the largest city in Central America.
Caribbean and Central America, north to.Managua: Managua sits beside a lake and several volcanic craters, and a 1972 earthquake destroyed much of its center.
Caribbean and Central America, north to.Port of Spain: Port of Spain, the capital of Trinidad and Tobago, hosts one of the world's most famous Carnivals and is the birthplace of steelpan music.
Caribbean and Central America, north to.Panama City: Panama City is where the Panama Canal meets the Pacific. It is unusual for having a tropical rainforest within its city limits.
Caribbean and Central America, north to.Bogotá: Bogotá lies high in the Andes at about 2,600 m, which makes it one of the highest capital cities in the world.

A journey toward the center of the Earth.Deepest known cave: Veryovkina Cave in Georgia's Abkhazia is over 2,200 metres deep.
A journey toward the center of the Earth.Deepest mine (Mponeng): A gold mine near Johannesburg where rock temperatures reach about 60 degrees, so ice slurry cools the air.
A journey toward the center of the Earth.Kola Superdeep Borehole: The Soviet borehole reached 12.26 km and stopped in 1992 when temperatures hit about 180 degrees.
A journey toward the center of the Earth.Bottom of continental crust: The Moho boundary was discovered by Andrija Mohorovičić in 1909.
A journey toward the center of the Earth.Bottom of the lithosphere: Tectonic plates are pieces of the lithosphere floating on the softer asthenosphere.
A journey toward the center of the Earth.Mantle transition zone: Minerals such as olivine change into denser forms here, and the zone may hold lots of water.
A journey toward the center of the Earth.Start of the lower mantle: The largest part of Earth by volume, made mostly of the mineral bridgmanite.
A journey toward the center of the Earth.Top of the outer core: Liquid iron and nickel; its churning creates Earth's magnetic field.
A journey toward the center of the Earth.Top of the inner core: It is solid despite extreme heat, because of the crushing pressure. It slowly grows as the core cools.
A journey toward the center of the Earth.Earth's center: At the centre, temperatures are about as hot as the Sun's surface and pressure is millions of atmospheres.

Famous cats, real and fictional, by year.The Cheshire Cat: Lewis Carroll's grinning cat from Alice's Adventures in Wonderland can vanish, leaving only its smile. The phrase "grin like a Cheshire cat" was already around.
Famous cats, real and fictional, by year.Felix the Cat: Felix was a huge star of silent cartoons, with merchandise worldwide. He was among the first characters to be a real global brand.
Famous cats, real and fictional, by year.Tom (Tom and Jerry): Hanna and Barbera's endless chase pair won multiple Oscars for their shorts. Tom and Jerry rarely speak.
Famous cats, real and fictional, by year.Sylvester: The lisping cat who chases Tweety was voiced by Mel Blanc, the "man of a thousand voices." A Tweety short won an Oscar in 1947.
Famous cats, real and fictional, by year.The Cat in the Hat: Dr. Seuss wrote it using only 236 different words, to answer a challenge for more fun early readers. The bold hat is now iconic.
Famous cats, real and fictional, by year.Top Cat: Top Cat leads a gang of alley cats in Manhattan and has the cunning of a TV sergeant. In the UK he was called Boss Cat.
Famous cats, real and fictional, by year.The Pink Panther: The pink cartoon cat first appeared in the opening credits of the 1963 comedy. Henry Mancini's jazzy theme song is famous worldwide.
Famous cats, real and fictional, by year.Garfield: Jim Davis's lasagna-loving cat is in Guinness World Records as the most widely syndicated comic strip. Mondays are his enemy.
Famous cats, real and fictional, by year.Larry, Downing Street's cat: Larry arrived at Number 10 from a rescue centre, and holds the title of Chief Mouser to the Cabinet Office. He has outlasted several prime ministers.
Famous cats, real and fictional, by year.Grumpy Cat: Her real name was Tardar Sauce, and her frown came from feline dwarfism and an underbite. She became a worldwide meme and a book star.

Famous opening lines, by year published.To be, or not to be: Shakespeare's Hamlet speech is often thought of as the most famous in English. The prince contemplates life and death with a skull.
Jane Austen's Pride and Prejudice opens with this wry line about money and marriage. It was published anonymously.
Moby-Dick sold poorly in Melville's lifetime. It is now seen as a masterpiece of American literature.
A Tale of Two Cities is set in London and Paris during the French Revolution. It's among the best-selling novels ever.
Famous opening lines, by year published.All happy families are alike: Tolstoy's Anna Karenina begins with a line about family misery. Scholars call the idea the Anna Karenina principle.
Tolkien reportedly scrawled this on a blank exam paper while marking. It became The Hobbit, about Bilbo Baggins.
Famous opening lines, by year published.A bright cold day in April: Orwell's 1984 starts with a cold day and the clocks striking thirteen. He finished writing it on the Scottish island of Jura.
Famous opening lines, by year published.Lolita, light of my life: Nabokov's controversial novel was first published in Paris because American publishers feared a scandal. It's now regarded as a classic.
Famous opening lines, by year published.As he faced the firing squad: The opening of One Hundred Years of Solitude jumps through time in one sentence. Gabriel García Márquez won the Nobel Prize in 1982.
Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone was rejected by a dozen publishers. The first print run was only about a thousand copies.

When these health organizations began.Nightingale nursing school: Florence Nightingale founded this school at St Thomas' Hospital in London. It made nursing a respected, trained profession.
When these health organizations began.St John Ambulance: It grew out of the Order of St John, and trains volunteers in first aid. Its volunteers staff events across the UK.
When these health organizations began.Macmillan Cancer Support: Douglas Macmillan founded it after his father died of cancer. The charity's nurses now help many cancer patients.
When these health organizations began.American Heart Association: Founded by doctors, it funds research into heart disease. Its logo is a flaming torch and a heart.
When these health organizations began.Alcoholics Anonymous: Two men, Bill W. and Dr. Bob, started it in Akron, Ohio. Its Twelve Steps have been widely copied for other addictions.
When these health organizations began.March of Dimes: President Franklin D. Roosevelt started it to fight polio, and people sent in dimes. After the Salk vaccine, it turned to birth defects.
When these health organizations began.Samaritans: Founded by a vicar, Chad Varah, in a London church. It offers a listening ear to people in distress, day or night.
When these health organizations began.Make-A-Wish: It began in Arizona when a seven-year-old boy with leukaemia dreamed of being a police officer. Local police made it happen.
When these health organizations began.Movember: It started in Melbourne with a few friends growing moustaches. It now raises funds for men's health worldwide.
When these health organizations began.Ice Bucket Challenge: Videos of people tipping buckets of icy water on themselves raised over $100 million for ALS research within weeks.

HBO series premieres.Oz: HBO's first one-hour drama, set in a prison, proved the network could make gritty original series.
HBO series premieres.Sex and the City: Based on Candace Bushnell's newspaper column, it ran six seasons and made cosmopolitans and Manolo Blahnik shoes famous.
HBO series premieres.The Sopranos: Often called the greatest TV drama ever; its abrupt cut-to-black ending in 2007 is still argued over.
HBO series premieres.Curb Your Enthusiasm: Larry David improvises from plot outlines rather than scripts; the show ended in 2024 after twelve seasons.
HBO series premieres.The Wire: Former Baltimore Sun reporter David Simon built it on the city's drug trade, ports, schools and newsroom.
HBO series premieres.Deadwood: Set in a South Dakota gold-rush camp, it features real figures such as Wild Bill Hickok and Al Swearengen.
HBO series premieres.True Blood: Based on Charlaine Harris's novels, it imagines synthetic blood letting vampires come out publicly.
HBO series premieres.Game of Thrones: Adapted from George R. R. Martin's novels, it ran eight seasons and was one of the most pirated shows ever.
HBO series premieres.Succession: Jesse Armstrong's drama about a feuding media dynasty ran four seasons and swept many Emmys.
HBO series premieres.The Last of Us: Adapted from Naughty Dog's video game, it brought the real cordyceps fungus, which controls ants, into a zombie story.

When these manuscripts were made.Dead Sea Scrolls (most): Found from 1947 in caves near Qumran, starting with a Bedouin shepherd, it includes the oldest known copies of Hebrew Bible books.
When these manuscripts were made.Codex Sinaiticus: One of the oldest nearly complete Christian Bibles, written in Greek and found at St Catherine's Monastery in Sinai.
When these manuscripts were made.Codex Argenteus: The 'Silver Bible' is a Gothic translation in silver ink on purple parchment, now kept at Uppsala University.
When these manuscripts were made.Lindisfarne Gospels: Made on Holy Island off Northumberland, it blends Celtic and Anglo-Saxon art, with Old English notes added later.
When these manuscripts were made.Book of Kells: This ornate gospel book is displayed at Trinity College Dublin, and its pages are covered in intricate Celtic art.
When these manuscripts were made.Beowulf manuscript: The only surviving manuscript of the Old English epic, singed in a 1731 library fire.
When these manuscripts were made.Domesday Book: William the Conqueror's survey of England; its name suggests the Day of Judgment, because there was no appeal against it.
When these manuscripts were made.Codex Gigas: The 'Devil's Bible' contains a full-page portrait of the devil, and legend says a monk wrote it in a night.
When these manuscripts were made.Hereford Mappa Mundi: The largest surviving medieval map, with Jerusalem at its center and east at the top.
When these manuscripts were made.Très Riches Heures: This illuminated prayer book for the Duke of Berry is famed for calendar pages showing seasonal peasant life.

US holidays, January to Labor Day.New Year's Day: Times Square's New Year's Eve ball has dropped since 1907, and millions watch it fall on television.
US holidays, January to Labor Day.Groundhog Day: The tradition of the groundhog comes from a German custom involving a badger, and Punxsutawney Phil has been predicting since 1887.
US holidays, January to Labor Day.Valentine's Day: Named for an early Christian martyr, it was linked with romance by Chaucer in the 14th century.
US holidays, January to Labor Day.St Patrick's Day: Chicago has dyed its river green every year since 1962.
US holidays, January to Labor Day.April Fools' Day: Nobody knows its origin for sure; one theory points to France's 16th-century change of New Year to January 1.
US holidays, January to Labor Day.Cinco de Mayo: It marks Mexico's 1862 victory over France at Puebla, not Mexican independence day, and it's bigger in the US than in Mexico.
US holidays, January to Labor Day.Mother's Day: Anna Jarvis campaigned for it, got a national holiday in 1914, and later turned against its commercial side.
US holidays, January to Labor Day.Father's Day: Sonora Smart Dodd's 1909 idea in Spokane led to its adoption, but Congress made it official only in 1972.
US holidays, January to Labor Day.Independence Day: John Adams expected 2 July to be the date; he and Thomas Jefferson both died on 4 July 1826, exactly 50 years on.
US holidays, January to Labor Day.Labor Day: Congress made it a federal holiday in 1894, days after the Pullman strike, and President Cleveland signed it.

Disney through the years.Disney studio founded: Walt and Roy Disney founded their cartoon studio in October 1923, first as the Disney Brothers Cartoon Studio in Hollywood.
Disney through the years.Mickey in Steamboat Willie: Steamboat Willie was among the first cartoons with fully synchronised sound, and its early Mickey became public domain in 2024.
Disney through the years.Snow White released: Snow White was nicknamed Disney's Folly while being made, since many believed audiences wouldn't sit through a feature-length cartoon.
Disney through the years.Disneyland opens: Disneyland opened in Anaheim, California on July 17, 1955, with an invitation-only day that famously went badly wrong.
Disney through the years.Walt Disney dies: Walt Disney died of lung cancer on December 15, 1966, and the studio was run by his brother Roy for years after.
Disney through the years.Walt Disney World opens: Walt Disney World covers about 40 square miles, which is larger than the island of Manhattan, and opened the Magic Kingdom first.
Disney through the years.Disney buys Pixar: Pixar began as Lucasfilm's computer division and was bought by Steve Jobs in 1986, before Disney paid about 7.4 billion dollars.
Disney through the years.Disney buys Marvel: Disney paid about 4 billion dollars for Marvel, then used the purchase to build the Marvel Cinematic Universe films.
Disney through the years.Disney buys Lucasfilm: Disney paid about 4 billion dollars for Lucasfilm, and soon released new Star Wars films like The Force Awakens in 2015.
Disney through the years.Disney+ launches: Disney+ signed up about 10 million users in its first day, and the service grew to over 100 million subscribers in just a couple of years.
